rewrites.prompt: A Windhoek sports shop sells a well-known brand of running shoe with a two-year guarantee. Explain the difference between the tangible and the intangible attributes of this shoe.
rewrites.canonical_answer: Tangible attributes can be examined before purchase; intangible ones cannot. The shoe's tangible attributes are its sole material, its weight, its stitching and its size range. Its intangible attributes are the brand's reputation for shoes that last, the status of being seen in it, and the two-year guarantee. The buyer pays for the whole bundle, so if the maker cheapened the sole or the shop shortened the guarantee, the value of the bundle would fall even though only one side of it was changed.
marking_guidance: 1 mark (AO1): the difference identified - whether the attribute can be physically examined before purchase.
2 marks (AO2): applied to the running shoe on both sides, with the consequence that the bundle loses value if either side is cut; 1 mark if one side only.
Boundary: both sides of the difference given for the same product.
rewrites.why: Distinguish is not used on the current AS papers; reworded to Explain at 3 marks - one difference, taken into a named business.

rewrites.prompt: A Swakopmund coffee shop has slightly better seating than its rivals, a friendlier welcome, and is the one shop in town that roasts its own beans. Explain the difference between product differentiation and a unique selling point for this coffee shop.
rewrites.canonical_answer: Differentiation is the general activity of making a product distinguishable from rivals, and it can be done in many small ways at once; a unique selling point is one claimable point of difference singled out of that and used as the centre of the message. The coffee shop's better seating and friendlier welcome differentiate it, but neither is distinctive enough to build a claim on. Roasting its own beans is a unique selling point: it can be stated, checked by customers and put at the centre of the shop's promotion.
marking_guidance: 1 mark (AO1): the difference identified - the general activity against one claimable point.
2 marks (AO2): applied to the coffee shop - small differences against the roasting as the claimable point; 1 mark for a generic example.
Boundary: the general activity against one claimable point; differentiation can exist without a unique selling point.
rewrites.why: Distinguish is not used on the current AS papers; reworded to Explain at 3 marks - one difference, taken into a named business.

rewrites.prompt: A Windhoek firm is launching two products: a patented water purifier and a new brand of maize meal. Explain the difference between price skimming and penetration pricing as launch strategies for these two products.
rewrites.canonical_answer: Skimming launches at a high price and lowers it in stages, taking a wide margin on low volume; penetration launches at a low price and aims to raise it later, taking a thin margin on high volume to win market share. Skimming suits the patented purifier: rivals cannot copy it at once, so the firm can sell first to the buyers least sensitive to price. Penetration suits the maize meal: it enters an established market full of similar brands, so a low price is what wins shelf space and buyers - though the firm will then have to raise the price from a base of customers who came for a bargain.
marking_guidance: 1 mark (AO1): the difference identified - the direction of the price, and margin against volume.
2 marks (AO2): applied to the two products - skimming for the patented purifier, penetration for the maize meal, with why each fits; 1 mark if only one is applied.
Boundary: both sides of the difference on the same dimensions.
rewrites.why: Distinguish is not used on the current AS papers; reworded to Explain at 3 marks - one difference, taken into a named business.

rewrites.prompt: A lodge near Sossusvlei charges Namibian residents less than international visitors, and raises both rates as it fills up. Explain the difference between dynamic pricing and price discrimination at this lodge.
rewrites.canonical_answer: Dynamic pricing varies the price with when a booking is made and the state of demand at that moment; price discrimination varies it with which group the buyer belongs to. The lodge's resident and international rates are price discrimination: two guests booking the same night at the same moment pay different amounts because one is a resident. Raising both rates as rooms fill is dynamic pricing: everyone booking at that moment sees the higher rate because the remaining capacity has fallen. So the boundary is what the difference is based on, and this lodge runs the two together on the same room.
marking_guidance: 1 mark (AO1): the difference identified - the basis of the price difference: timing and demand against the buyer's group.
2 marks (AO2): applied to the lodge's two rates and how both move as it fills; 1 mark for a generic example.
Boundary: the basis of the difference, not the existence of two prices.
rewrites.why: Distinguish is not used on the current AS papers; reworded to Explain at 3 marks - one difference, taken into a named business.

rewrites.prompt: An Ondangwa hardware shop buys a spade for N$40 and prices it using a 25% mark-up. Explain the difference between the shop's mark-up percentage and the amount it adds to the price of each spade.
rewrites.canonical_answer: The mark-up is a percentage of cost - here 25% of the N$40 the spade cost the shop. The amount added is the money that percentage produces: 25% of N$40 is N$10, so the spade sells for N$50. The difference matters because the percentage is fixed by the shop's pricing rule, while the money amount depends on the cost it is applied to: if the supplier's price rises to N$48, the same 25% mark-up adds N$12 and the spade sells for N$60.
marking_guidance: 1 mark (AO1): the difference identified - a percentage of cost against the money amount it adds.

2 marks (AO2): applied to the spade - 25% of N$40 adding N$10 for a price of N$50, and how the amount changes with the cost while the percentage does not; 1 mark if the figures are stated without the contrast.
Boundary: the percentage against the money amount, with the cost named as the base.
rewrites.why: Distinguish is not used on the current AS papers; reworded to Explain at 3 marks. Also resolves the scope audit: the card now stays on mark-up (cost-plus pricing, 3.3) instead of contrasting it with profit margin, which the syllabus places at A Level (10.2.2).

rewrites.prompt: A Windhoek bookshop works out a price of N$101 for a new novel from its cost and its usual mark-up, then puts N$99.95 on the cover. Explain the difference between cost-based pricing and psychological pricing in how this price was set.
rewrites.canonical_answer: Cost-based pricing takes the business's own cost figure as its reference point and adds a mark-up to it; psychological pricing takes the buyer's reading of the number as its reference point. The bookshop used cost-based pricing to reach N$101, a figure produced from inside the business. Moving to N$99.95 is psychological pricing: it asks how buyers will read the number, betting that a price below N$100 is heard as belonging to a lower band. That is why psychological pricing is usually applied last, as an adjustment to a price another method produced.
marking_guidance: 1 mark (AO1): the difference identified - the reference point each method uses.
2 marks (AO2): applied to the novel - N$101 from cost and mark-up, N$99.95 for how buyers read it; 1 mark for a generic contrast.
Boundary: the reference point; the two are usually applied in sequence rather than as alternatives.
rewrites.why: Distinguish is not used on the current AS papers; reworded to Explain at 3 marks - one difference, taken into a named business.

rewrites.prompt: A Namibian mobile network runs a television campaign and also a stand in an Oshakati shopping centre that gives away SIM cards. Explain the difference between above-the-line and below-the-line promotion, using these two activities.
rewrites.canonical_answer: Above-the-line promotion is paid communication placed in media the business does not control; below-the-line promotion is communication the business controls directly, with no independent media owner in between. The television campaign is above the line: the network buys airtime and takes whatever audience the channel delivers, reaching many people but making it hard to trace which viewers then signed up. The shopping-centre stand is below the line: the network runs it itself and reaches far fewer people, but can count exactly how many SIM cards it handed out and how many were activated.
marking_guidance: 1 mark (AO1): the difference identified - whether an independent media owner stands between the business and its audience.
2 marks (AO2): applied to the television campaign and the shopping-centre stand, with the contrast in reach and measurement; 1 mark if one side only.
Boundary: the difference stated on both sides.
rewrites.why: Distinguish is not used on the current AS papers; reworded to Explain at 3 marks - one difference, taken into a named business.

rewrites.prompt: A new pharmacy in Katima Mulilo advertises its opening hours and prices on local radio, in an advertisement voiced by a well-known presenter. Explain the difference between informative and persuasive advertising, using this advertisement.
rewrites.canonical_answer: Informative advertising sets out facts the buyer needs - what is sold, what it costs, where to get it; persuasive advertising works on preference and image, aiming to be chosen over a rival. The pharmacy's opening hours, prices and address are informative, which suits a new business whose listeners do not yet know it exists. Using a well-known presenter's voice is persuasive: it borrows trust and familiarity to make this the pharmacy people choose. So one advertisement can carry some of both.
marking_guidance: 1 mark (AO1): the difference identified - facts the buyer needs against preference and image.
2 marks (AO2): applied to the pharmacy's radio advertisement, showing both in one campaign; 1 mark for a generic example.
Boundary: fact against preference; most real campaigns contain both.
rewrites.why: Distinguish is not used on the current AS papers; reworded to Explain at 3 marks - one difference, taken into a named business.

rewrites.prompt: A Namibian manufacturer makes cooldrink, a professional-grade paint and electric bicycles. Explain the difference between intensive, selective and exclusive distribution for these three products.
rewrites.canonical_answer: The difference is how many outlets carry the product, which trades availability against the producer's control over how it is sold. Cooldrink suits intensive distribution: it is bought on impulse, so it needs to be in as many outlets as possible. The professional paint suits selective distribution through a limited number of trade merchants whose staff can advise contractors. The electric bicycles suit exclusive distribution through one dealer per town, which protects the dealer's margin and the standard of servicing at the cost of being harder to find.
marking_guidance: 1 mark (AO1): the difference identified - the number of outlets, as a trade-off between availability and control.
2 marks (AO2): applied to the three products, with a fitting level of intensity for each; 1 mark if only one or two are applied.
Boundary: the three are distinguished by that trade-off.
rewrites.why: Distinguish is not used on the current AS papers; reworded to Explain at 3 marks - one difference, taken into a named business.

rewrites.prompt: A learner writes that the 4Ps are a checklist a business works through in order. Explain the error and correct it.
marking_guidance: The correction must say the elements constrain one another, not merely that all four matter.
Reward an example of one element forcing a change in another.
A discrimination card: it corrects a stated error, which the papers do not set as a question, so it carries no paper tariff.
rewrites.why: State is not used on the current AS papers; reworded to Explain and kept as a discrimination card with no paper tariff.

rewrites.prompt: A learner writes that a restaurant is a service business and therefore sells no goods. Explain the error and correct it.
marking_guidance: The correction must say most offerings blend the two rather than that a restaurant is really a goods business.
Reward the reformulated question about where the value sits.
A discrimination card: it corrects a stated error, which the papers do not set as a question, so it carries no paper tariff.
rewrites.why: State is not used on the current AS papers; reworded to Explain and kept as a discrimination card with no paper tariff.

rewrites.prompt: Identify the stages of the product life cycle in order, and what happens to sales in each.
marking_guidance: The five stages must be given in the correct order, beginning with development.
Start from what the model takes as given: sales measured against time.
State what happens to sales at each step, not only the stage name.
The answer should end with decline and what happens to sales there.
A recall card: it asks for the whole sequence, which the papers ask for one point at a time, so it carries no paper tariff.
rewrites.why: State is not used on the current AS papers; reworded to Identify and kept as a recall card with no paper tariff.

rewrites.prompt: Identify the four functions of packaging.
marking_guidance: All four functions are required, each stated with a precise sense of what it does.
The identification function is the one that makes packaging part of promotion.
A recall card: it asks for all four functions, which the papers ask for one item at a time, so it carries no paper tariff.
rewrites.why: State is not used on the current AS papers; reworded to Identify and kept as a recall card with no paper tariff. Define was the work order's target, but the card asks for a list, not a meaning.
